title: The Runes
otherNames: futhark (fuþark), from its first six letters
family: Germanic runic alphabets. They are not a learned cipher. Most scholars derive them from a Mediterranean alphabet, most often a North Italic (Alpine) one; the Latin and Greek alphabets are the other candidates.
summary: The runes are the native alphabet of the early Germanic peoples. The earliest securely dated inscription is the Vimose comb from Denmark, c. 160 CE. There are three main rows: the 24-letter Elder Futhark (in use to about 700–800), the Anglo-Saxon futhorc (expanded to 28 or more letters) and the 16-letter Younger Futhark of the Viking Age. Most surviving inscriptions are memorials, ownership marks and messages. A smaller group seems to be for protection, cursing or healing: bracteate words such as alu and laukaz, the Blekinge curse stones and the Ribe skull fragment. In the thirteenth century the Eddic poems present runes as a power that Óðinn won, and Egils saga shows its hero carving them to curse and to heal. Guido von List's 18 'Armanen' runes (1908) and most present-day rune divination are modern creations, and the SS took some runes as emblems.

firstAttestation.work: Vimose comb, a bone or antler comb with the runic inscription harja (read as a personal name, a tribal name or a word for 'comb'; the sense is disputed)
firstAttestation.author: anonymous
firstAttestation.date: c. 160 CE (Rundata DR 207; some secondary sources give c. 150)
firstAttestation.locator: Rundata DR 207 (also Krause–Jankuhn no. 26; DK Fyn 19); National Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen, inv. 22657, as given in the Rundata record
firstAttestation.notes: Several early objects compete for 'first'. The Meldorf brooch (Schleswig-Holstein; dated by type to the first half of the 1st century CE; rediscovered in 1979 in the stores at Schloss Gottorf) has four incised signs whose reading is disputed: runic hiwi (Düwel and Gebühr 1981), Latin IDIN (Odenstedt 1989; Seebold 1994) or runic iṛiḷi (Mees 1997). If runic, it would be more than a century older than Vimose. The Svingerud stone (Hole, Ringerike, Norway) was announced in January 2023 by the Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo, which dated it to 1–250 CE from burnt bone and charcoal in the cremation pit and called it the oldest datable runestone. A 2025 article in Antiquity treats the find as fragments of one slab, possibly carved on different occasions, and dates the grave contexts more widely, to between 50 BCE and 275 CE. The Øvre Stabu spearhead (Norway, raunijaz; Rundata N KJ31) is dated between about 160 and 260 CE, depending on the source. The first complete row of all 24 runes is on the Kylver stone, Gotland (Rundata G 88, c. 400 CE, a date taken from the grave). It is a limestone slab from a grave at Kylver, Stånga parish, excavated in 1903, and is in the Swedish History Museum (Statens historiska museum), Stockholm. Its row reads … j p ï z … ŋ d o and is followed by a tree-like sign, read by some as stacked t-runes. The palindrome sueus stands apart from the row. The inscription was on the underside of the slab, facing into the grave. Reading that placement as a message for the dead is an interpretation; the inscription itself neither confirms nor refutes it.

transmission.work: Earliest inscriptions (Vimose comb, DR 207, c. 160; Øvre Stabu spearhead, Norway, raunijaz, N KJ31, dated between c. 160 and c. 260 depending on the source)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The first securely runic texts, mostly short: names, maker's or owner's words, weapon names.

transmission.work: Kylver stone (Rundata G 88), Stånga, Gotland
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The first complete futhark row: 24 runes in a fixed order, the earliest evidence that the row was learned as a sequence. Kylver reads … h n i j p ï z s … l ŋ d o. It has p before ï and d before o, the reverse of both pairs on the Vadstena bracteate.

transmission.work: Gold bracteates (Vadstena, Ög 178; Grumpan, Vg 207; and many others)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Gold pendants modelled on Roman imperial medallions. Vadstena (found 1774, c. 500 CE; stolen from the Swedish History Museum in 1938 and never recovered) and Grumpan (found 1911, 6th century; damaged at the eyelet, where z and s are lost) divide the futhark into three groups of eight with dots, the later ættir. Others carry short formulas such as alu, laþu, laukaz, auja. These are the centre of the debate on 'rune magic'.

transmission.work: Blekinge stones: Stentoften (DR 357) and Björketorp (DR 360)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Curse formulas in the transitional runic of southern Sweden. They threaten anyone who breaks the monument and name 'runes of power' (ginArunAz) hidden there. Björketorp is usually dated to the 6th or 7th century. Hanna Åkerström (Futhark, 2025) argues that the usual reading order of Stentoften should be revised.

transmission.date: c. 600 (Noleby; not later than c. 450–600 on its language and rune forms) and c. 800 (Sparlösa)
transmission.work: Noleby stone (Vg 63) and Sparlösa stone (Vg 119), Västergötland
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Inscriptions calling runes 'derived from the gods' (raginaku(n)do; rægi[n]kundu). The same word, reginkunnum, appears in Hávamál 80 (Neckel–Kuhn numbering; Bellows orders stanzas 79 and 80 differently).

transmission.work: Transition to the Younger Futhark (16 runes); Rök stone (Ög 136), early 9th century
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The row was cut to 16 runes, each covering several sounds, in long-branch ('Danish') and short-twig ('Swedish-Norwegian') forms. Rök, with about 760 runes, is the longest runic inscription on stone. Parts of it are enciphered, by substituting runes and by special cipher runes.

transmission.date: c. 725 (deposited 725–750 according to a 2013 dating study)
transmission.work: Ribe skull fragment (Denmark)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: A piece of human skull with a hole bored through it, inscribed with the names Ulfr, Óðinn and Hō-Tīwʀ ('High-Týr'). The older reading takes them as help against 'this pain' and a 'dwarf' (a disease-spirit). Jackie Nordström (2021) reads help against a male and a female dwarf. Staffan Fridell (2024) disputes the dwarf reading. It is the clearest early protective or healing charm, but its wording is contested.

transmission.work: Anglo-Saxon futhorc on objects (Franks Casket, 8th century, Northumbria; Ruthwell Cross; Seax of Beagnoth or Thames scramasax, 10th century per the British Museum, with the only complete 28-rune row, in an irregular order)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The English expanded the row to 28 runes, and manuscripts go up to about 33 (Page 1999; not checked in this run), adding ōs, āc, æsc, ȳr, īor, ēar and others. The poet Cynewulf signed four poems with runes: Elene and The Fates of the Apostles in the Vercelli Book, and Juliana and Christ II in the Exeter Book.

transmission.work: Abecedarium Nordmannicum (St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. Sang. 878, p. 321); Vienna, ÖNB Cod. 795 (Gothic letter names)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Learned Carolingian records of runes. The Abecedarium Nordmannicum names the 16 Younger runes in a mixture of Old Saxon, Old High German and Norse. The page was damaged in the 19th century by chemicals meant to preserve it, and the text is known partly through Wilhelm Grimm's drawing of 1828. Vienna 795 preserves names for the letters of the Gothic alphabet. Their language differs from Wulfila's, and some scholars doubt how far they can be relied on. These names, with the rune poems, are the basis for reconstructing the Elder names.

transmission.date: composition disputed (estimates from the 7th to the 10th century); manuscript lost 1731; printed 1705
transmission.work: Old English Rune Poem (formerly in London, BL, Cotton Otho B.x)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 29 stanzas, one per futhorc rune, each beginning with the rune name: Christian, gnomic and mnemonic. The manuscript, Cotton Otho B.x (fols 165a–165b), was lost in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731. The text survives only through Humfrey Wanley's copy as printed by George Hickes, Linguarum veterum septentrionalium thesaurus (Oxford, 1703–05), vol. I (1705), p. 135. Since the early 20th century some scholars have questioned how faithfully Hickes's print reproduces the lost manuscript.

transmission.date: probably early 13th century (composition); medieval manuscript lost 1728
transmission.work: Norwegian Rune Poem (Rúnakvæði)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 16 couplets on the Younger Futhark, each pairing the rune name with an unrelated proverb. The medieval manuscript was lost in the Copenhagen fire of 1728. The poem survives through Ole Worm's print in Runir (1636) and late 17th-century copies, the most authoritative by Árni Magnússon and Jón Eggertsson.

transmission.date: c. 1220–1240 (second quarter of the 13th century); main manuscript Möðruvallabók, AM 132 fol., c. 1330–70
transmission.work: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar (attributed to Snorri Sturluson by many scholars on stylistic grounds, an idea argued systematically by Björn M. Ólsen in 1904; the attribution is debated)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: In the saga, Egill carves runes and reddens them with his blood so that a poisoned horn bursts (ch. 44). He carves runes on a scorn-pole (níðstöng) to curse King Eiríkr and Queen Gunnhildr (ch. 57). He cures a sick girl by scraping off a botched rune charm on whalebone and carving a new one (ch. 72). The chapter numbers are those of Íslenzk fornrit II; W. C. Green's 1893 translation puts the horn episode in ch. 45. These are literary episodes written about two centuries after the events.

transmission.work: Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Reykjavík, Árni Magnússon Institute, GKS 2365 4to; in Copenhagen until its return to Iceland on 21 April 1971)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Contains Hávamál, Sigrdrífumál and Skírnismál. In Neckel–Kuhn numbering, Hávamál 138–145 (Rúnatal) tells how Óðinn hung nine nights on the tree and 'took up the runes', and 146–163 (Ljóðatal) lists 18 charms; stanza 164 is often taken as a later addition. Some editions number these 139–146 and 147–165. Sigrdrífumál lists kinds of runes and where to carve them. Skírnismál 36 threatens a þurs-rune curse; editors divide the stanzas of that passage differently. This is the main literary source for rune magic, and it is late and poetic.

transmission.date: c. 1500 and later (AM 687d 4to, c. 1500; AM 461 12mo, c. 1550)
transmission.work: Icelandic Rune Poem
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 16 short stanzas of kennings, recorded in four Arnamagnæan manuscripts. Each is followed by a Latin word (fé = aurum, Týr = Mars, etc.) and a Norse word for 'chieftain' that alliterates with the rune name. These glosses are given from the standard editions (Dickins 1915; Page 1999) and were not checked in this run. The central part of the text in AM 687d 4to is badly damaged.

transmission.work: Johannes Bureus (Johan Bure, 1568–1652), Swedish royal antiquary: the engraved runic sheet Runakänslanes lärespån (Elementa runica, 1599), the Runa ABC (1611) and the manuscript Adulruna rediviva
transmission.author: Johannes Bureus
transmission.what: The first learned 'rune esotericism'. Bureus recorded runestones as an antiquary. He also built a Gothicist, Kabbalistic and Hermetic system of 15 'Adulrunes', which he called a 'Kabala Upsalica' or 'Notaricon Suethica' and worked out in several versions of Adulruna rediviva over some forty years (one source dates the first to 1605). A study of Kabbalah in Sweden names Agrippa, Paracelsus and Reuchlin among his models, and he read John Dee's Monas hieroglyphica in 1610. He is the closest point of contact between runes and the Agrippan, Christian-Kabbalist tradition (Karlsson 2010; Åkerman 1998).

transmission.work: Ole Worm, Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima (1636); Danicorum monumentorum libri sex (1643)
transmission.author: Ole Worm
transmission.what: Antiquarian publications in Latin. Runir (1636; 2nd ed. 1651) printed runic alphabets and texts, including the Norwegian Rune Poem. Danicorum monumentorum libri sex (1643) published the Danish runestones. With Bureus's work in Sweden, these made runic monuments a subject of Latin scholarship.

transmission.work: Guido von List, Das Geheimnis der Runen (first as a periodical article, 1906; as a book, 1908, no. 1 of the Guido-von-List-Bücherei)
transmission.author: Guido von List (1848–1919)
transmission.what: Introduces the 18-rune 'Armanen' row (fa ur thurs os rit ka hagal not is ar sig tyr bar laf man yr eh gibor). List claimed that it came to him in a revelation during some eleven months of blindness after a cataract operation in 1902, and he keyed it to the 18 charms of Hávamál's Ljóðatal. Historians treat it as a modern creation. It is the root of most völkisch and later occult rune systems. The place and publisher of the 1908 book are given differently in different sources (see factcheck).

transmission.work: Völkisch rune occultism and National Socialist use
transmission.author: F. B. Marby, S. A. Kummer, R. J. Gorsleben, K. M. Wiligut; the SS and the Ahnenerbe (founded 1935; one source gives 1936)
transmission.what: 'Rune gymnastics' and 'rune yoga' (Marby, Kummer) developed out of List. The SS emblem, a doubled 'Sig' rune drawn by Walter Heck (1929 or 1933; sources differ), was adopted in the early 1930s. The SS also used the Odal rune and the 'life' and 'death' runes. Wiligut, Himmler's adviser, designed the SS Totenkopfring (SS-Ehrenring) with runic signs. Runology in this period was entangled with the regime (Mees 2008; Goodrick-Clarke 1985).

transmission.date: 1982 (some records give 1983 for the first US edition)
transmission.work: Ralph Blum, The Book of Runes (Oracle Books / St. Martin's Press)
transmission.author: Ralph Blum
transmission.what: A popular rune-casting oracle sold with a set of rune tiles. It adds a blank rune (called 'Odin') and reorders the row. It is the source of much present-day divinatory rune meaning, and it is modern.

transmission.work: The Unicode Standard: Runic block U+16A0–U+16FF (Unicode 3.0); U+16F1–U+16F8 added in Unicode 7.0
transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Encodes the Elder, Anglo-Saxon, Younger and medieval runes in one unified block. 7.0 added Tolkien's runes and the Franks Casket variants. The block also has the calendar symbols arlaug, tvímaðr and belgþor (U+16EE–U+16F0), used for golden numbers 17–19 on runic calendars.

claims.claim: The runes were adapted from a Mediterranean alphabet, most probably a North Italic (Alpine) alphabet of the Etruscan family.
claims.evidence: Several letter shapes and the left- or right-running direction match North Italic alphabets. Ludvig Wimmer (Runeskriftens oprindelse, 1874) derived the runes from the Latin capitals. Otto von Friesen (from 1904–06) and Sophus Bugge argued for a Greek script borrowed by the Goths, which the dates make hard to sustain; Bugge had earlier favoured a North Etruscan source. The North Italic thesis (Carl Marstrander, in the first volume of Norsk tidsskrift for sprogvidenskap, 1928) is the most widely held, but there is no consensus.

claims.claim: The word 'rune' meant 'secret, mystery' before it meant 'letter'.
claims.evidence: Gothic rūna translates Greek mystērion in Wulfila's Bible (e.g. Mark 4:11). Old English rūn means 'secret, counsel, whisper', and Old Irish rún, a Celtic cognate, means 'secret'. This is lexical evidence only. It does not show that the letters were themselves secret or magical.

claims.claim: Hávamál tells that Óðinn won the runes by hanging nine nights on a wind-swept tree, wounded by a spear and 'given to Óðinn, myself to myself'.
claims.evidence: Hávamál 138–139 (Neckel–Kuhn numbering; 139–140 in Bellows, who moves the manuscript's closing stanza ahead of the Rúnatal) in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270). The poem is the only witness. Its date of composition is unknown, and it was written down in Christian Iceland.

claims.claim: Runes were held to be of divine origin.
claims.evidence: Some carvers say so themselves. Noleby stone (Vg 63, c. 600; not later than c. 450–600): runo fahi raginakudo (also transcribed raginaku(n)do), 'I paint/write the rune derived from the gods'. Sparlösa (Vg 119, c. 800): rúnaR … rægi[n]kundu. Hávamál 80 (Neckel–Kuhn) later uses the same word: rúnum … reginkunnum. Cleasby–Vigfússon alone glossed the word as 'universally known'. The belief is documented; the origin itself is legend.
sources: Mees, 'The Noleby inscription', Arkiv för nordisk filologi

claims.claim: The word alu, frequent on bracteates and other early objects, is a magical or protective formula.
claims.evidence: alu appears alone or in formulas on many 5th–6th-century bracteates, on the Elgesem stone (Vestfold, Norway; found 1870; Rundata N KJ57, c. 400), on the Lindholm amulet (Skåne), and stamped on cremation urns at Spong Hill, Norfolk. Proposed meanings include 'ale' (Old Norse ǫl, Old English ealu, perhaps a ritual drink), 'protection' or 'sanctuary' (compare Gothic alhs 'temple'), and a link to Hittite words for 'bewitched' (Polomé). Most runologists accept that it was a cultic or amuletic word but do not agree on its sense.

claims.claim: The word laukaz 'leek' on bracteates is a fertility or prosperity charm.
claims.evidence: laukaz and abbreviations of it occur on many bracteates. The Fløksand find (Nordhordland, Norway; a knife or scraper from a woman's grave, found 1864) reads lina laukaz, 'linen [and] leek' (some transcribe laukar). Two literary parallels are cited. In Völsa þáttr, preserved only in Flateyjarbók, a preserved horse-phallus is wrapped in linen with leeks and herbs (the link is discussed by Wilhelm Heizmann and Klaus Düwel in Völsi-Geschichten, 2021). Sigrdrífumál 8 tells the reader to throw a leek into the cup against poison. Egill's verse calls the sick girl 'linden of leeks' (lauka lindi). That the word worked as a charm is an interpretation; that it was written on amulets is documented.

claims.claim: Futhark rows written out on objects (Kylver, the Vadstena and Grumpan bracteates) were magical in purpose.
claims.evidence: Some scholars read a complete row as an amulet, like Latin abecedaria on late-antique amulets. Others read it as a writing exercise or a display of literacy. Kylver's grave context (the inscription on the underside of the slab, facing into the grave) is sometimes read in favour of the first reading for that stone, but the inscription itself neither confirms nor refutes this.

claims.claim: Runes were used for curses on monuments.
claims.evidence: Björketorp (DR 360) and Stentoften (DR 357) threaten whoever breaks the stone. In the compiler's paraphrase of Björketorp: 'runes of power hidden here; restless through sorcery, to an insidious death, is he who breaks it'. Danish 10th-century stones such as Glavendrup (DR 209, Funen, early 10th century) read 'Þórr vígi þessi rúnaR', 'may Thor hallow these runes', and end with a curse on whoever damages the stone or drags it away to stand in memory of another (reading of the National Museum of Denmark). On other stones the formula refers to the monument instead of the runes.

claims.claim: Runes were used in healing charms.
claims.evidence: The Ribe skull fragment (c. 725) invokes Ulfr, Óðinn and Hō-Tīwʀ. Its sense, help against 'pain and a dwarf' or against a male and a female dwarf, is debated (Nordström 2021; Fridell 2024). The Sigtuna amulet I (copper, 11th century, found 1931) is a charm against 'wound-fever'. It addresses a þurs (or Þórr; the reading is disputed) and a 'wolf' (Ulfr), the same name as the person it was made for (Hall 2009). Many medieval lead amulets carry runic charms. Egils saga ch. 72 (ÍF II) describes a healing charm on whalebone, but that is literature, not evidence of practice.

claims.claim: Medieval Christian Scandinavians wrote learned Latin and Hebrew-derived charms in runes (Ave Maria, Pater Noster, the SATOR square, AGLA).
claims.evidence: Such charms appear on runic amulets and on sticks from Bryggen in Bergen (12th–14th c.). The Bryggen stick N 636 begins 'agla' and continues with SATOR AREPO and the names of the archangels Raphael, Gabriel and Michael (Rundata). AGLA, the Pater noster and the Ave Maria are common on Norway's medieval lead amulets. This is where runes meet the Latin magical tradition the rest of the Magical Scriptorium follows.

claims.claim: Egils saga tells that Egill Skalla-Grímsson cured a girl by re-carving runes that an unskilled man had cut wrongly on a whalebone.
claims.evidence: Egils saga (written c. 1220–1240), ch. 72 in Íslenzk fornrit II; other translations may number the chapters differently. The saga reports the episode with a skaldic verse attributed to Egill (Skaldic Project: Egill Lausavísur 40). It shows what 13th-century Icelanders thought about runes, not what 10th-century people did.

claims.claim: Tacitus describes the Germans casting runes for divination.
claims.evidence: Germania 10 (98 CE) describes cutting a branch of a fruit-bearing tree into slips, marking them with 'certain signs' (notis quibusdam), scattering them on a white cloth, and reading three. Tacitus does not say what the signs were. No inscription confirms runic lots, and the earliest runes are about half a century later than Tacitus. The Latin of the passage is confirmed against transcriptions of Germania 10.

claims.claim: The Elder Futhark has known traditional names and meanings for each rune.
claims.evidence: No Elder Futhark name list survives. The names are reconstructed (asterisked) from the Old English Rune Poem, the Norwegian and Icelandic poems, the Abecedarium Nordmannicum and the Gothic letter names in Vienna, ÖNB Cod. 795. Several are uncertain: *perþ-, *algiz, *kaunan or *kenaz, *laguz or *laukaz. The poems' meanings are medieval and often differ from one another.

claims.claim: The rune poems are magical texts.
claims.evidence: Their form is mnemonic and gnomic: name, then proverb or kenning. The Old English poem is explicitly Christian ('if he wishes to gain glory before the Lord'). Modern occult use treats them as keys to rune meanings, but nothing in them describes magical use.

claims.claim: List claimed that the 18 Armanen runes were revealed to him and preserved a lost Aryan priestly wisdom.
claims.evidence: This is List's own claim in Das Geheimnis der Runen (article 1906; book 1908): a revelation during about eleven months of blindness after a cataract operation in 1902, as Flowers reports in the introduction to his 1988 translation. No inscription or manuscript uses this row. It reworks the 16 Younger runes with two additions (eh, gibor) and keys them to the charms of Hávamál's Ljóðatal. Historians (Goodrick-Clarke) treat it as a modern creation within Ariosophy.

claims.claim: The SS and other National Socialist bodies used runes as insignia.
claims.evidence: The doubled 'Sig' rune of the SS (drawn by Walter Heck; 1929 or 1933, sources differ); the Odal rune (SS Race and Settlement Main Office and other units); and the 'life' and 'death' runes (ᛉ upright and inverted), used for the Lebensborn and, in obituaries and on gravestones, to mark dates of birth and death in place of the asterisk and cross. These uses drew on List's tradition. In Germany, public display of Nazi emblems was first banned under Allied occupation law after 1945. The Assembly Act of 1953 penalised showing the emblems of former National Socialist organisations. The ban entered the Criminal Code as §96a in 1960 and has been §86a StGB since the Eighth Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1968; it covers the SS runes. In June 2026 the Bavarian Higher Regional Court (BayObLG 206 StRR 137/26, as reported by beck-aktuell) held a Sig-rune-style letter on a demonstration poster punishable. Today the Odal and 'life' runes also appear in far-right iconography, and the same letters are used without such meaning by historians, by modern Heathen religious groups, and in ordinary Scandinavian use.
sources: Deutscher Bundestag, Wissenschaftliche Dienste, 'Das strafbare Verwenden von Kennzeichen verfassungswidriger Organisationen'

claims.claim: The blank 'Odin' rune and the standard modern divinatory meanings are ancient.
claims.evidence: The blank rune is generally credited to Ralph Blum's The Book of Runes (1982; some records give 1983), which sold rune tiles with a blank 'Odin' tile. That it first appears there rests on secondary and popular sources and was not checked against a first edition. Divinatory meanings come from 20th-century occult writers working from the medieval rune poems. No ancient source describes divination with individual runes.

claims.claim: erilaz, a title on several early inscriptions ('ek erilaz …'), means 'rune-master' or 'magician'.
claims.evidence: It has been connected to the Heruli, to the jarl rank, and to a professional class of carvers. Its sense is unknown.

claims.claim: Runes were mainly a magical script.
claims.evidence: Against: most of the corpus is memorial stones, ownership and maker's marks, and, at Bryggen, business letters, love notes and jokes. In the 6th century Venantius Fortunatus mentions runes painted on ash tablets as a plain way to send a letter. R. I. Page wrote that a runologist needs both imagination and scepticism, that in practice runologists lean to one side or the other, and counted himself among the sceptics (An Introduction to English Runes, 2nd ed. 1999, pp. 12–13, as cited in a review; the wording was not checked). For: amuletic formulas, curse stones and healing charms do exist (above). The fair statement is that runes were an ordinary script that was also used for magic.

letters.name: *fehu ('cattle, movable wealth')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with two parallel straight branches on its right, both sloping UP to the right. The upper branch leaves the stave a little below its top, about a quarter of the way down, and rises to end about level with the stave's top. The lower branch leaves the stave about half-way down and rises parallel to it, ending further out to the right and at or a little below the top line. No ring-ends. Compare the a-rune (no. 4), whose branches start at the top and slope down. Font note: Noto Sans Runic draws the two branches as curves, both ending on the top line, the lower one reaching about twice as far out as the upper. Set the letter in the font, or draw this straight handbook form, but do not mix the two.
letters.note: It survives into the Younger Futhark and the futhorc with the same sound and the same name, 'wealth', in all three rune poems. Unicode: U+16A0 RUNIC LETTER FEHU FEOH FE F. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: the compiler's form put the upper branch's root at the top of the stave while sloping it upward, which is geometrically impossible within the band; corrected against Noto Sans Runic (fontsource 5.3.0, runic subset), outlines extracted in this project.]
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER FEHU FEOH FE F

letters.name: *ūruz ('aurochs (wild ox)')
letters.form: An angular inverted U. A full-height stave stands on the left. From its top, a straight stroke slopes down to the right. A second leg, starting lower, about a quarter to a third of the way down, drops vertically or slightly slanted to the baseline. The rune is about half as wide as it is tall. Some early inscriptions round the top.
letters.note: The name differs between the poems. Old English has 'aurochs', the Norwegian poem 'slag', the Icelandic 'drizzle'. *ūruz is a modern reconstruction. Unicode: U+16A2 RUNIC LETTER URUZ UR U. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: Noto Sans Runic rounds the shoulder into an arch, and its right leg's straight part begins about half-way down; the angular form described is the handbook form.]

letters.name: *þurisaz ('giant (þurs)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with a pointed triangular bow on its right, at mid-height. A straight stroke leaves the stave about a third of the way down and runs down-right to a point about a third of the height out. A second straight stroke returns down-left to the stave about two-thirds down. The stave closes the triangle. Some inscriptions round the bow or set it higher.
letters.note: This is the 'þurs' rune that Skírnir threatens to carve in Skírnismál 36 (see quotations). The Norwegian poem says þurs 'causes the sickness of women', and the Icelandic poem calls it 'the torment of women'. Unicode: U+16A6 RUNIC LETTER THURISAZ THURS THORN. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: Noto Sans Runic draws a large rounded bow running from about an eighth below the top to an eighth above the foot; the triangular mid-height bow described here is the angular handbook form. Do not mix the two.]

letters.name: *ansuz ('a god (one of the Æsir)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. On its right, two parallel straight branches slope DOWN and to the right. The upper branch starts at the top of the stave, the lower about a third of the way down. Each reaches out about a third of the height. Compare the f-rune (no. 1), whose branches rise. (Matches Noto Sans Runic.)
letters.note: In the Anglo-Saxon futhorc this form split into ōs ᚩ, āc ᚪ and æsc ᚫ. In the Younger Futhark the rune stands for a nasal a/o. The Norwegian poem reads óss as 'estuary', the Icelandic poem as 'god'. Unicode: U+16A8 RUNIC LETTER ANSUZ A. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

poemNames.oldEnglish: ōs (the futhorc gives this name to a new rune ᚩ)

letters.name: *raidō ('riding, journey')
letters.form: An angular capital R. A full-height stave. From its top, a straight stroke runs down-right to a point. A second stroke returns down-left to the stave at about mid-height, enclosing a triangular pocket. From that junction, a straight leg runs diagonally down-right to the baseline and ends below the pocket's outer point.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16B1 RUNIC LETTER RAIDO RAD REID R. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: in Noto Sans Runic the pocket's return stroke stops just short of the stave and meets the leg there, leaving the pocket open towards the stave; many inscriptions close it.]
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER RAIDO RAD REID R

letters.name: *kaunan (or *kenaz) ('ulcer, sore (Norse); torch (Old English)')
letters.form: In the oldest inscriptions it is not full height. It is a small angle like '<': two short straight strokes meet at a point on the left and open to the right. Many early inscriptions set it high in the writing band; Noto Sans Runic centres it just above mid-height, spanning from about a quarter to about four-fifths of the height. Many fonts draw ᚲ at full height. Later forms differ: the Younger kaun ᚴ is a stave with one branch rising to the right from its middle (curved in Noto Sans Runic). Take the Anglo-Saxon cēn ᚳ from the font or a handbook table (see note).
letters.note: Both names, *kaunan and *kenaz, are reconstructions. Handbooks differ on which to print. The Old English and Norse poems give different senses. Unicode: U+16B2 RUNIC LETTER KAUNA. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: the compiler described Anglo-Saxon cēn ᚳ as 'a stave with two branches falling from its top'. Noto Sans Runic instead draws a stave with one branch running from its lower middle down to the baseline on the right. The description is withdrawn until checked against Page 1999. The size and height of the early '<' vary between inscriptions and tables, so formConfidence is lowered to medium.]

letters.name: *gebō ('gift')
letters.form: Two full-height straight diagonals that cross at the centre: an X filling the band. There is no stave.
letters.note: The Younger Futhark dropped it, so there is no Norse rune-poem stanza for it. Unicode: U+16B7 RUNIC LETTER GEBO GYFU G. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *wunjō ('joy')
letters.form: An angular P. A full-height stave with a closed triangular flag on its upper right. A straight stroke runs from the stave's top down-right to a point. A second returns down-left to the stave about half-way down (a little below half in Noto Sans Runic).
letters.note: The Anglo-Saxon wynn passed into Old English book-hand as the letter ƿ (wynn), which scribes used for w. Unicode: U+16B9 RUNIC LETTER WUNJO WYNN W. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *hagalaz ('hail')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves joined by one straight crossbar. The bar runs diagonally from the upper part of the left stave down to the lower part of the right stave. Continental and Anglo-Saxon inscriptions often have two parallel crossbars instead (ᚻ, U+16BB, 'haegl'). The Younger Futhark has the different forms ᚼ and ᚽ.
letters.note: Which form appears where is the compiler's recollection of the handbooks (single bar in Scandinavia, double bar on the continent and in England); check it against Barnes 2012 or Düwel 2008. Unicode: U+16BA RUNIC LETTER HAGLAZ H. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *naudiz ('need, constraint')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave crossed at mid-height by one short straight stroke that slopes down from left to right. The stroke projects a little on both sides of the stave.
letters.note: Sigrdrífumál 7 tells the reader to mark 'Nauð' on the fingernail as an ale-rune (see quotations). Unicode: U+16BE RUNIC LETTER NAUDIZ NYD NAUD N. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER NAUDIZ NYD NAUD N

letters.name: *īsaz ('ice')
letters.form: A single full-height vertical stave.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16C1 RUNIC LETTER ISAZ IS ISS I. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER ISAZ IS ISS I

letters.name: *jēra ('year, (good) harvest')
letters.form: The standard (Unicode) form: two separate angular hooks set on a diagonal. Each hook is two short straight strokes meeting at an angle. One sits upper-left, the other lower-right. Each opens towards the other. They overlap in height across the middle of the band but do not touch. Early inscriptions vary more on this rune than on any other: some put a stave through the middle, some round the hooks.
letters.note: Old j became a in the Younger Futhark (ár), because Proto-Norse lost initial j-, so *jāra became ár. The Anglo-Saxon gēr has its own form ᛄ (U+16C4). Unicode: U+16C3 RUNIC LETTER JERAN J. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: matches Noto Sans Runic, where the upper-left hook is a '<' and the lower-right hook a '>'. The whole rune is small and sits high, from about a third of the height up to the top line.]

letters.name: *ī(h)waz / *eihwaz ('yew')
letters.value: Ï (a vowel near i or e; value disputed)
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. A short straight stroke runs from its top, slanting down to the right, about a fifth of the height. A matching stroke runs from its foot, slanting up to the left. The figure is point-symmetric, like a stretched S or Z on a vertical spine. Mirror forms also occur, with the top branch to the left.
letters.note: Its sound value is one of the open questions of runology. The yew name passed to a different rune in the Younger Futhark (see no. 15). Unicode: U+16C7 RUNIC LETTER IWAZ EOH. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: the form matches the Noto Sans Runic outline.]

poemNames.norwegian: (dropped; the Younger yew-name ýr went to the z/R-rune)

letters.name: *perþ- (meaning unknown) ('unknown')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with a V-shaped notch at each end on its right. At the top, a short straight stroke runs from the stave's top down-right to a point about a sixth of the height down, and a second short stroke runs from that point up-right to end on the top line: a V opening upward. At the foot the figure is mirrored: from the stave's foot a stroke runs up-right to a point about a sixth of the height up, and a second runs down-right to end on the baseline: an inverted V opening downward. The outer ends stand about half the stave's height out from it. The right side is open across the middle.
letters.note: It is the rarest rune of the row and is almost absent from early inscriptions. The meaning of peorð is unknown (guesses include a dice-cup, a pear tree or a game). [Fact-check: the compiler's form (two short strokes turning straight down and up towards each other, like a cup on its side) did not match the Noto Sans Runic outline and was replaced. The form above follows the Noto glyph, which agrees with published verbal descriptions (a stave with two short strokes at top and bottom, turned away from each other). Inscriptional forms vary, and Kylver's p was not checked.] Unicode: U+16C8 RUNIC LETTER PERTHO PEORTH P. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *algiz (reconstruction uncertain) ('elk? protection?')
letters.value: Z, later R (final -z of Proto-Germanic, later a palatal r)
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. Two straight branches spring from it between half and two-thirds of the way up. They rise diagonally up-left and up-right and end about level with the stave's top: an upward fork like a trident or Greek psi. Some Elder inscriptions invert it, with the branches pointing down. The inverted form became standard as Younger ýr ᛦ (U+16E6).
letters.note: This is the rune modern writers call the 'life rune' (Lebensrune). As a symbol it was used in National Socialist Germany, e.g. by the Lebensborn organisation, and with its inverted form in obituaries and on gravestones for dates of birth and death; see claims and cautions. The rune poems do not support a reading as 'protection'. Unicode: U+16C9 RUNIC LETTER ALGIZ EOLHX. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: the form matches the Noto Sans Runic outline.]

letters.name: *sōwilō ('sun')
letters.form: A vertical zigzag of straight strokes, like a lightning flash, with no stave. Noto Sans Runic draws four strokes of equal length. Starting on the top line at the right, the first runs down-left to the left edge about a quarter of the way down. The second runs down-right to the right edge at mid-height, the third down-left to the left edge three-quarters of the way down, and the fourth down-right to the baseline at the right. The result is a W turned on its side, a little under half as wide as it is tall. Many handbook tables print a three-stroke form instead: a short steep stroke, a longer diagonal running back across, and a second short steep stroke. Inscriptions have from three to about eight strokes, in either orientation.
letters.note: Copy the exact form from the Noto Sans Runic glyph if the page sets the font; inscriptions vary too much for one 'correct' drawing. The SS emblem is described as a doubled 'Sig' rune, a name taken from List's Armanen row; its zigzag resembles the s-runes (see claims). In the Younger Futhark the s-rune is ᛋ (long-branch) or ᛌ (short-twig). Unicode: U+16CA RUNIC LETTER SOWILO S. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *tīwaz ('the god Tiw / Týr')
letters.form: An upward arrow. A full-height stave with two short straight strokes falling from its top, one to the left and one to the right. They reach down about a fifth to a third of the height (a fifth in Noto Sans Runic).
letters.note: Sigrdrífumál 6 says victory-runes are carved on the sword-hilt, 'naming Týr twice'. Many scholars connect that line to this rune. Unicode: U+16CF RUNIC LETTER TIWAZ TIR TYR T. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: Sigrdrífumál 6 reads 'ok nefna tysvar Tý'; confirmed.]
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER TIWAZ TIR TYR T

poemNames.oldEnglish: Tīr (in the poem, a guiding star or sign)
poemNames.icelandic: Týr ('the one-handed god'; Latin gloss Mars)

letters.name: *berkanan ('birch (twig)')
letters.form: An angular capital B. A full-height stave with two closed triangular bows on its right, one above the other. Two straight strokes go out from the stave's top to a point and back to its middle. Two more go out from the middle to a point and back to the foot. Early forms sometimes separate the bows slightly or round them.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16D2 RUNIC LETTER BERKANAN BEORC BJARKAN B. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER BERKANAN BEORC BJARKAN B

letters.name: *ehwaz ('horse')
letters.form: An angular M with a shallow middle. Two parallel full-height staves. A straight stroke runs from the top of the left stave down-right to a point midway between them, about a third of the height down. A second rises from that point to the top of the right stave. The middle V does not reach the baseline.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16D6 RUNIC LETTER EHWAZ EH E. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *mannaz ('man, human being')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves with two straight diagonals crossing between them in the upper half. One runs from the top of the left stave to about mid-height on the right stave. The other runs from the top of the right stave to about mid-height on the left. Together they make an X between the staves.
letters.note: The Younger Futhark m is a different form: ᛘ (long-branch) or ᛙ (short-twig). Unicode: U+16D7 RUNIC LETTER MANNAZ MAN M. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *laguz (or *laukaz) ('water, lake (or leek)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with one short straight branch. It leaves the top of the stave and slopes down to the right for about a fifth to a third of the height (a fifth in Noto Sans Runic).
letters.note: Some runologists reconstruct the Elder name as *laukaz 'leek', not *laguz 'water', because laukaz is a common word on bracteates. This is a disputed proposal. The rune poems all give the 'water' name. Unicode: U+16DA RUNIC LETTER LAUKAZ LAGU LOGR L. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER LAUKAZ LAGU LOGR L

letters.name: *ingwaz ('the god Ing (Yngvi)')
letters.form: A closed square standing on one corner (a diamond, ◇). It is usually smaller than the other runes and set in the upper part or middle of the band. Some inscriptions draw it full height or put it on a stave. The Anglo-Saxon form ᛝ (U+16DD) is a diamond whose sides run on into crossing tails.
letters.note: Size and position vary between the early rows. The compiler could not check Kylver's form in this run. Unicode: U+16DC RUNIC LETTER INGWAZ. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: Noto Sans Runic draws a ring with clipped corners, centred at mid-height and about half the band high.]

poemNames.oldEnglish: Ing (a hero or god 'first seen among the East Danes')

letters.name: *dagaz ('day')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves joined by two straight diagonals that cross at the centre. One runs from the top of the left stave to the foot of the right stave, the other from the top of the right stave to the foot of the left. The result looks like an hourglass lying on its side, closed by the two staves.
letters.note: On Kylver, d comes before o. On some bracteate rows and in the Old English poem it comes after o (ēþel, then dæg). Unicode: U+16DE RUNIC LETTER DAGAZ DAEG D. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *ōþalan / *ōþila ('inherited land, ancestral estate')
letters.form: A diamond (a square on its corner) filling the upper two-thirds of the band. Its two lower sides run on past the bottom corner, cross there, and continue as two short legs splayed down-left and down-right to the baseline. There is no stave.
letters.note: This is the 'odal rune'. In National Socialist Germany a variant was used by the SS Race and Settlement Main Office and by other units. A variant with serifs or 'wings' appears in post-war far-right iconography. The plain letter form above is the historical one. Do not print the winged variant. Unicode: U+16DF RUNIC LETTER OTHALAN ETHEL O. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested. [Fact-check: the plain form matches the Noto Sans Runic outline (diamond filling the upper two-thirds). The use of a variant by the SS Race and Settlement Main Office was not confirmed in this run.]

lettersSource: The Elder Futhark, 24 runes in three ættir of eight, in the conventional modern order of the handbooks (Barnes 2012; Düwel 2008). That order follows the Vadstena and Grumpan bracteates for … i j ï p z … (Kylver has p before ï) and Kylver for the ending … ŋ d o (Vadstena has … ŋ o d). Some editions print … ŋ o d, as in the Old English poem's ēþel–dæg. Characters, code points and Unicode names come from the Runic block U+16A0–U+16FF and were checked against the Unicode Character Database 14.0 (Python unicodedata) by the compiler and again by the fact-checker, with no mismatch. The glyphs should be set in Noto Sans Runic (@fontsource/noto-sans-runic 5.3.0, runic subset U+16A0–16F8; see understand.md §7), not drawn. The 'form' fields describe the normalised angular forms of the handbooks, with the main inscriptional variants, so the page can explain a shape or check the font. The forms were not traced from any single inscription. The fact-checker compared every form with the Noto Sans Runic outlines. Noto differs from the angular handbook forms in four places: ᚠ ᚢ ᚦ are curved, the ᚱ pocket is open towards the stave, ᛊ has four strokes, and ᚲ ᛃ ᛜ differ in size or height. Each difference is noted on its letter. Rune-poem names follow Dickins 1915 and Halsall 1981. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions. Runes have no numerical values in the early tradition, so numeric is null. Supporting rows are given under youngerFuthark, futhorcAdditions and armanenRow (the last for the 'modern invention' panel only).

armanenRow.note: Guido von List's 1908 row of 18, as listed in Goodrick-Clarke 1985 and in the Flowers translation. Show it as a modern invention, with names only. Do not draw it with the SS or other organisational stylings.

uses.use: Everyday writing: memorials, ownership and maker's marks, letters and messages
uses.evidence: This is the bulk of the corpus. Viking-Age memorial stones in Sweden, Denmark and Norway; the Bryggen sticks of Bergen (12th–14th c.); and Venantius Fortunatus, Carmina VII.18, to Flavus (6th c.; c. 585 by one dating), on runes painted on ash tablets for letters.
Words such as alu, laþu, laukaz, auja ('luck') and gibu auja ('I give luck') on 5th–6th-century gold bracteates and other objects. The sense is disputed (see claims).
Björketorp and Stentoften (Blekinge, 6th–7th c.); Danish 'Þórr vígi' stones such as Glavendrup (DR 209, early 10th c.).
The Ribe skull fragment (c. 725; reading debated); the Sigtuna amulet I (11th c.); medieval lead amulets; and, in literature, Egils saga ch. 72 (ÍF II).

uses.use: Christian and learned charms written in runes
uses.evidence: Latin prayers, the SATOR square and AGLA on medieval runic amulets and sticks, e.g. Bryggen N 636 (MacLeod & Mees 2006; Rundata). This is the overlap with the Latin and Hebrew magical traditions of the rest of the wing.

uses.use: Eddic 'rune-craft': victory, ale, birth, sea, limb, speech and mind runes
uses.evidence: Sigrdrífumál 6–13 names each kind and where to carve it. Stanza 18 (Neckel–Kuhn) says the runes were shaved off and mixed into the holy mead, the same scraping-off Egill performs. Hávamál 144 asks whether the reader knows how to carve (rísta), interpret (ráða), stain (fá), test (freista), ask, sacrifice, send and slay. This is literary and late, but it is the main textual source for a magical understanding of runes.

uses.use: Mnemonic and poetic use of the rune names
uses.evidence: The three rune poems; Cynewulf's runic signatures; Old English riddles that use runes.
The cipher runes on the Rök stone (early 9th c.), and the medieval Icelandic and Scandinavian traditions of coded runes built on the three ættir.

Medieval and early modern perpetual calendars on staves and boards use the 16 Younger runes plus three extra signs (arlaug, tvímaðr, belgþor) for the 19 golden numbers. Unicode encodes these as U+16EE–U+16F0.

There is no ancient evidence for divination with individual runes. Tacitus's lots (Germania 10) carried unspecified signs. Present-day rune divination draws on 20th-century writers: List (1908) gave each rune an esoteric meaning, and Blum (1982) popularised casting rune tiles.

uses.use: Early modern learned esotericism and modern occultism
uses.evidence: Johannes Bureus's Adulruna (17th c.); List's Armanen runes (1908) and the völkisch rune-occultists of the 1920s–30s; post-war Heathen and occult use (reported only, not reproduced).

quotations.text: I ween that I hung | on the windy tree, / Hung there for nights full nine; / With the spear I was wounded, | and offered I was / To Othin, myself to myself, …
quotations.translation: Henry Adams Bellows (trans.), The Poetic Edda (New York: American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923; public domain), Hovamol stanza 139. These lines were matched in searches of the sacred-texts.com and voluspa.org copies of Bellows; check punctuation against the 1923 printing (Project Gutenberg #73533) before print. The stanza's last two lines are not quoted; in paraphrase, the tree is one whose roots no one knows. Original Old Norse (normalised; the first five lines confirmed against Pettit's dual-language edition, Open Book Publishers 2023): 'Veit ek, at ek hekk / vindga meiði á / nætr allar níu, / geiri undaðr / ok gefinn Óðni, / sjálfr sjálfum mér, / á þeim meiði, / er manngi veit / hvers af rótum renn.' Bellows numbers it 139 because, following Müllenhoff, he moves the manuscript's closing stanza ahead of the Rúnatal.
quotations.source: Hávamál 138 (Neckel–Kuhn numbering; Bellows 139), Codex Regius GKS 2365 4to

quotations.text: Við hleifi mik sældu / né við hornigi; / nýsta ek niðr, / nam ek upp rúnar, / æpandi nam, / fell ek aptr þaðan.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse (normalised; phrases matched against the voluspa.org edition) with a partial published translation. Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923), Hovamol stanza 140, renders the central lines 'I took up the runes, | shrieking I took them' (matched against the sacred-texts.com copy). The rest of his wording was not confirmed. In the fact-checker's paraphrase: no one gave me bread or drink; I peered down, took up the runes, took them screaming, and fell back from there.

quotations.text: Þat er þá reynt, / er þú at rúnum spyrr / inum reginkunnum, / þeim er gerðu ginnregin / ok fáði fimbulþulr.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase, not a published translation: 'It is proven, when you ask about the runes of divine descent, which the mighty powers made and the great sage coloured [painted].' Spelling of 'gerðu/gørðu' varies with the normalisation. Some editions, Bellows among them, number this stanza 79.

quotations.text: Veiztu hvé rísta skal? / Veiztu hvé ráða skal? / Veiztu hvé fá skal? / Veiztu hvé freista skal? / Veiztu hvé biðja skal? / Veiztu hvé blóta skal? / Veiztu hvé senda skal? / Veiztu hvé sóa skal?
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Do you know how to carve? how to read [interpret]? how to colour? how to test? how to ask? how to offer? how to send? how to slaughter [sacrifice]?' Some editions spell 'Veistu'. The stanza is in málaháttr metre.

quotations.text: Sigrúnar skaltu kunna, / ef þú vilt sigr hafa, / ok rísta á hjalti hjǫrs, / sumar á véttrimum, / sumar á valbǫstum, / ok nefna tysvar Tý.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Victory-runes you must know if you want victory, and carve them on the sword's hilt, some on the blade-guards, some on the blade, and name Týr twice.' The two blade terms are of uncertain meaning.
quotations.source: Sigrdrífumál 6 (Neckel–Kuhn), Codex Regius; text as in Pettit 2023 and voluspa.org

quotations.text: Ǫlrúnar skaltu kunna, / ef þú vill annars kvæn / véli-t þik í tryggð, ef þú trúir; / á horni skal þær rísta / ok á handar baki / ok merkja á nagli Nauð.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Ale-runes you must know if you do not want another man's wife to betray your trust; carve them on the horn and on the back of the hand, and mark Nauð [the n-rune] on the nail.'

quotations.text: Full skal signa / ok við fári sjá / ok verpa lauk í lǫg.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'The cup must be blessed, and guarded against harm, and a leek thrown into the liquid.' This is the literary parallel to laukaz on the bracteates. Some editions read 'lauki í lǫg'.

quotations.text: Þurs ríst ek þér / ok þrjá stafi, / ergi ok æði / ok óþola; / svá ek þat af ríst, / sem ek þat á reist, / ef gørask þarfar þess.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'A þurs [the þ-rune] I carve for you, and three staves: lust and frenzy and unbearable longing. I can carve it off as I carved it on, if there is need.' Editors divide the stanzas of this passage differently (the manuscript order is disturbed), so the stanza number varies.

quotations.text: Skalat maðr rúnar rísta, / nema ráða vel kunni; / þat verðr mǫrgum manni, / es of myrkvan staf villisk; / sák á telgðu talkni / tíu launstafi ristna; / þat hefr lauka lindi / langs ofrtrega fengit.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'A man should not carve runes unless he can read them well; many a man goes astray over a dark letter. I saw ten secret staves carved on the whittled whalebone; they have brought the linden of leeks [the woman] long, heavy grief.' The opening and the phrase 'lauka lindi' were matched against the Skaldic Project text (Egill Lausavísur 40). Published translations: Hermann Pálsson & Paul Edwards (Penguin Classics, 1976); Bernard Scudder, in The Complete Sagas of Icelanders I (1997).
quotations.source: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar, ch. 72 (Íslenzk fornrit II, ed. Sigurður Nordal, 1933); Skaldic Project, Egill Skalla-Grímsson, Lausavísur 40

quotations.text: virgam frugiferae arbori decisam in surculos amputant eosque notis quibusdam discretos super candidam vestem temere ac fortuito spargunt.
quotations.translation: Original Latin with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree into slips, mark them with certain signs, and scatter them at random over a white cloth.' The signs are not said to be runes. A published English version: M. Hutton, revised E. H. Warmington, Loeb Classical Library (1970). The Latin wording of the opening was matched against transcriptions of Germania 10.

quotations.text: barbara fraxineis pingatur runa tabellis, / quodque papyrus agit, virgula plana valet.
quotations.translation: Original Latin with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Let the barbarian rune be painted on tablets of ash; what papyrus does, a smoothed stick can do.' Evidence for runes as an ordinary means of correspondence. Some editions print 'rhuna' for 'runa'. The poem's number (Carm. VII.18, Ad Flavum) is confirmed in the Latin texts.
quotations.source: Venantius Fortunatus, Carmina VII.18 (to Flavus), 6th c.

quotations.text: Feoh byþ frofur fira gehwylcum; / sceal ðeah manna gehwylc miclun hyt dælan / gif he wile for drihtne domes hleotan.
quotations.translation: Original Old English (wording confirmed against the CLASP corpus and other transcriptions of Hickes's text) with the fact-checker's own paraphrase: 'Wealth is a comfort to everyone; yet each must share it out freely if he wants to win glory before the Lord.' Bruce Dickins's 1915 translation is the standard English rendering, but its wording could not be tied to Dickins in this run and is not quoted.
quotations.source: Old English Rune Poem, stanza 1 (feoh); text from Hickes's Thesaurus, 1703–05

quotations.text: Wealth is a source of discord among kinsmen; the wolf lives in the forest.
quotations.translation: Bruce Dickins (trans.), Runic and Heroic Poems of the Old Teutonic Peoples (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1915), Norwegian Rune Poem, stanza 1; matched against the Wikisource transcription of Dickins. The Old Norse original is not reproduced, because its spelling could not be confirmed against an edition in this run.

quotations.text: [Paraphrase, not a quotation] Wealth is strife among kinsmen, the fire of the flood and the path of the serpent; followed by the Latin gloss aurum and the Norse word fylkir, 'chieftain'.
quotations.translation: The fact-checker's paraphrase of the stanza as edited by Dickins (1915) and Page (1999). Neither the Old Icelandic wording nor Dickins's English could be confirmed in this run, so neither is quoted.

Proto-Norse original as transliterated in the handbooks, with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'I paint (write) the rune derived from the gods.' The reading runo fahi raginakudo is confirmed (Rundata; Mees); some transcribe raginaku(n)do.

quotations.text: izwis atgiban ist kunnan runa þiudangardjos gudis
quotations.translation: Gothic original with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'to you it is given to know the mystery (runa) of the kingdom of God.' It shows rūna = Greek mystērion. The Gothic wording is confirmed against the wulfila.be text of Mark 4.

links.relation: One of the three candidate parents (Wimmer 1874). Medieval Scandinavians also wrote Latin prayers and charms in runes, and Ole Worm and Bureus made rune study part of Latin learning.
Another proposed parent (Bugge; von Friesen), now generally rejected on chronology. Gothic rūna translates Greek mystērion.
The remote ancestor, through Greek and the Etruscan or North Italic alphabets.

AGLA, a notarikon of Hebrew 'Atah gibbor le-olam Adonai', appears on medieval runic amulets, and Bureus's Adulruna drew on Christian Kabbalah. This is where the runic tradition meets the Hebrew-based magical alphabets.

Both appear in modern 'magical alphabet' lists and in modern witchcraft, but they have unrelated histories. Theban is a cipher alphabet keyed to Latin. It was first printed in Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518), which ascribes it to Honorius of Thebes on the authority of Pietro d'Abano (no such passage is known in d'Abano's surviving works), and Agrippa reprinted it in De occulta philosophia III.29. The runes are a native script. Do not present them as one tradition.

To check, not to assert. The pseudo-Hrabanus treatise De inventione litterarum (also cited as De inventione linguarum; manuscripts of the 8th–9th centuries) gives runes as the letters of the Marcomanni, 'whom we call Nordmanni'. A study of Trithemius's sources says that in Polygraphia VI (1518) he adopted some of the alphabets exemplified by Hrabanus. Whether a runic 'Nordmannic' alphabet is among them was not confirmed in this run.

Contrast only. Icelandic galdrastafir (magical staves, e.g. in the Galdrabók, 16th–17th century, and the Huld manuscript, 1860) are sign-magic like the charaktêres and are not runes, although they sometimes include runes. The vegvísir is first known from the Huld manuscript. The name ægishjálmur occurs in the Eddic Fáfnismál, but the drawn sign comes from late manuscripts. Neither sign dates from the Viking Age. (The dates come from secondary sources; check them against a scholarly edition.)

cautions: This file was compiled without web search and fact-checked with web search on 2026-10-20 (see factcheck). The Unicode code points and names were checked mechanically (UCD 14.0), and the letter forms against the Noto Sans Runic outlines. Items listed in factcheck.unresolved are still unverified. Check each against the named edition, or leave it out, before publication.

Stanza and chapter numbers differ between editions. Hávamál 138 in Neckel–Kuhn is 139 in Bellows (confirmed: Bellows moves the manuscript's closing stanza ahead of the Rúnatal); Larrington's numbering was not checked. Bellows also orders Hávamál 79–80 differently. Egils saga chapters here follow Íslenzk fornrit II (horn ch. 44, scorn-pole ch. 57, whalebone ch. 72); W. C. Green's 1893 translation puts the horn in ch. 45. Always cite the edition.
Mark the Proto-Germanic names (*fehu, *ansuz …) as reconstructions on the page. Only the rune-poem and manuscript names are attested, and those are medieval.
Do not present the modern divinatory meanings, the blank rune, the 'Armanen' row, 'rune yoga' or the vegvísir as ancient. Report them under 'modern', with dates.

Sensitive symbols: the doubled Sig-rune, the Odal rune with 'wings' or serifs, the 'life/death' runes in SS styling, and the Wolfsangel (not a rune) are prohibited in some contexts in Germany (StGB §86a) and appear in hate-symbol databases. Show runes only as letters in their historical rows, in a neutral typeface. Report the Nazi-era use soberly and in its own section. Do not reproduce insignia. German courts apply §86a to look-alike forms: in June 2026 the Bavarian Higher Regional Court (BayObLG 206 StRR 137/26, as reported by beck-aktuell) held a Sig-rune-style letter on a demonstration poster punishable.

Do not reproduce the emblems or texts of living organisations: modern Heathen bodies such as Ásatrúarfélagið (recognised in Iceland since 1973), or rune-occult orders. They may be named, but not illustrated.

The Codex Regius poems (c. 1270) and Egils saga (c. 1220–40) were written in Christian Iceland, centuries after the Elder Futhark went out of use. They are evidence for medieval ideas about runes, not for Migration-Period practice.

Agrippa prints the Theban alphabet in De occulta philosophia III.29, and the Transitus fluvii (with the Celestial and Malachim scripts) in III.30. These locators come from the Theban and Passing-the-River reference entries and the chapter headings of the 1651 English translation. Neither the compiler nor the checker knows of a runic alphabet anywhere in De occulta philosophia, but that absence could not be confirmed by search. The runes enter the learned-magic lineage through Bureus (17th c.) and the medieval Latin charms written in runes, so the wing should not imply an Agrippan pedigree.

Stephen E. Flowers (Runes and Magic, 1986) is an academic runologist who also writes on rune occultism as Edred Thorsson. Cite his dissertation for formula data, and pair it with sceptical runologists (Page, Barnes) on interpretation.
Wikipedia, Omniglot and rune-divination sites are not sources for history here. The Unicode chart is a source for code points only.

letters[3] thurisaz: the form is kept as the handbook form, with a note that the Noto glyph's bow is rounded and much taller.
letters[4] ansuz: 'the mirror of the f-rune' was imprecise and is replaced by a plain comparison. The form matches Noto.

letters[6] kaunan: 'sits in the upper half of the band' is qualified, since Noto centres it. The compiler's description of Anglo-Saxon ᚳ ('two branches falling from its top') does not match the Noto glyph (one branch from the lower middle to the baseline) and is withdrawn. formConfidence is lowered from high to medium.
letters[8] wunjo: the flag's depth is changed from 'a third to half' to 'about half' (Noto: a little below half).

letters[14] perþ: the compiler's form (ends turning straight down/up towards each other, 'a cup on its side') contradicts the Noto Sans Runic outline: a V notch at the top and an inverted V at the foot, with the outer strokes turned away from each other. It is rewritten to the Noto form; formConfidence stays medium, with the reason stated.

letters[16] sowilo: the compiler gave a three-stroke 'standard form', but Noto Sans Runic draws four equal strokes. Both forms are now described. 'The doubled Sig rune was drawn from this rune' is replaced by the documented naming (List's 'Sig').
letters[17] tiwaz and letters[21] laguz: branch length widened to 'a fifth to a third' to match the Noto outline.
lettersSource: the Kylver/Vadstena order statement is corrected. The Noto Sans Runic comparison and its four kinds of difference are added, and the UCD re-check is recorded.

uses: Glavendrup dated to the early 10th century; Ribe's reading marked as debated; Bryggen N 636 cited; Sigrdrífumál 18 confirmed; List's part in divination described more precisely (he assigned meanings, he did not teach casting).

quotations[0] Hávamál 138: the Bellows wording, given 'from memory', is now quoted only as far as the search matched it (the first four lines); the closing lines are paraphrased. The Old Norse is confirmed (Pettit 2023), and the stanza-number offset is explained.

quotations[4] Sigrdrífumál 6: 'nefna tvisvar Tý' corrected to the edited reading 'nefna tysvar Tý'.

quotations[11] OE feoh: the English attributed to Dickins 'from memory' is withdrawn, because the matching web copies do not name the translator. The confirmed Old English is kept with a labelled paraphrase.
quotations[12] Norwegian fé: the Dickins English is confirmed and is now the quotation. The Old Norse, which could only be matched on a non-scholarly page, is withdrawn until checked.
quotations[13] Icelandic fé: neither the Old Icelandic text nor the Dickins English could be confirmed; both are replaced by a labelled paraphrase.

links[theban]: 'Theban is a learned 1518 alphabet' implied it was made in 1518 and passed over its attribution. It now reports its first printing (Trithemius 1518), the ascription to Honorius via Pietro d'Abano as an ascription, and Agrippa III.29.

links[trithemius]: the pseudo-Hrabanus attribution and the Marcomanni/Nordmanni wording are confirmed, and so is Trithemius's use of Hrabanus's alphabets in Polygraphia VI. Whether Polygraphia prints the runic one stays open.
links[charakteres]: the Huld manuscript dated (1860); the Eddic occurrence of the name ægishjálmur distinguished from the late drawn sign.

cautions: the 'no web search' disclaimer is replaced by the fact-check record. The Bellows numbering offset is confirmed and explained, and the Egils saga chapter numbers are given. Agrippa III.29 (Theban) and III.30 (Transitus/Celestial/Malachim) are confirmed as locators; the absence of runes is still flagged. A 2026 §86a ruling is added to the sensitive-symbols caution.
